replying_to: Replying to Distributional Inclusion Vector Embedding for Unsupervised Hypernymy Detection

content.title: Review
content.review:
This work proposes DIVE (distributional inclusion vector embeddings), an unsupervised method for hypernymy discovery that preserves the inclusion property of old fashioned sparse BOW representations (i.e., that hypernyms tend to have higher counts in more varies contexts than hyponyms). The learned representations are evaluated on a large set of datasets and are shown to work well. The work is very thorough, and almost reads as a systematic study in places. Unfortunately, this makes it hard to follow sometimes, and although the work is generally interesting, I am left to wonder about its novelty and general impact on the field.

The main proposition essentially comes down to a slight tweak in word2vec's SGNS method: instead of shifting the PMI value of word co-occurrences by 1/k, we shift by #w/(k*|D|/|V|) and add a non-negativity constraint, i.e., we explicitly force Eq. 2 to be true in perfect reconstructions. This makes sense and I am surprised nobody has done it before. It feels like a minor tweak, however, and any major improvement seems to be largely dependent on the scoring function, rather than on this slightly different objective. Consequently, I feel like the paper is in two minds about what it wants to be: a systematic study of hypernymy detection methods, or an introduction of a novel algorithm for learning distributional inclusion embeddings.

I like the main ideas of this work and I think it's great that the study is so thorough, but I don't think it should be accepted in its current form. Main concerns:

- Presentation: the experiments show that (1) DIVE outperforms GE, HyperScore and H-Feature baselines; (2) which scoring function works best for DIVE; (3) DIVE outperforms SBOW in many cases, but not always, though better on average; and (4) we can use DIVE for WSD (only shown qualitatively). The paper spans 13 pages, excluding appendices, which is rather long. I feel that (2), (3) and (4) are part of a systematic study/review paper, while (1) could be interesting in and of itself, if it included a full comparison against alternative methods. The way results are presented in the tables is confusing, and it's unclear why only one baseline is included in each case.

- Comparison: it appears that there are methods missing from the results tables. On HyperLex, for example, results as high as 0.512 (Poincare embeddings), 0.540 (HyperVec) and 0.686 (LEAR) have been reported, while the highest result in the paper is 34.5. That's a big difference. On Weeds' BLESS, it's 68.6 versus e.g. 0.75 for Kiela et al. (unsupervised, using images) and 0.850 for HyperVec. If these results were omitted due to space, I think experiment (2) and (4) can safely be moved to the appendix. Especially for something that hinges on being a review paper, such as this work, it is important to be complete.

In short, I think the presentation doesn't help; I am left to wonder what the main contribution is of the work; and I think the comparison to previous work is incomplete.

Questions:
- Why use WaCkypedia? It's old and, by now, small. It would be interesting to try all scoring functions and types of model (PPMI, PPMI with shift, PPMI with inclusion shift) trained on the exact same corpus and same negatives, and showing that it works best there.
- General question: Is Vendrov's test set only yes/no, e.g. if I set the threshold really low, I get 100% accuracy, or does it contain negatives? Same for BLESS. If so how valuable is this evaluation?
- To what extent are the baselines tuned in the semi-supervised case? If the numbers are from papers, that should be mentioned. It would be better to use the same corpus, and the same amount of attention to tuning the results, for both cases.

Minor/Typos:
- Medicl
- "From the recent review (Santus et al) ... suggested by the review study (Vulic et al)" this way of citing reviews isn't very pretty
content.confidence: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature

display_title: This paper focuses on the unsupervised setting

content.title: This paper focuses on the unsupervised setting
content.comment:
Comment 1: Not comparing DIVE with some baselines

Response 1: This work proposes an unsupervised method which uses only the raw text of a corpus to detect hypernyms. Like we admitted in the first experiment (now moved to Section A.1), (semi-)supervised methods will perform better when models are trained on lots of annotated lexicon pairs (e.g., all hypernym relations from WordNet). Take the HyperLex as an example, 0.512 (Poincare embeddings) and 0.540 (HyperVec/HyperScore) are achieved by training model on ~700k hypernymy relations and ~2M hypernymy relations, respectively; 0.686 (LEAR) requires ~1.5M hypernymy relations, ~1M synonymy pairs, and ~380k antonymy pairs. The experiment setups of these (semi-)supervised methods are too different from us to be comparable. 

Although the method proposed in Kiela et al. does not require annotated lexicon pairs, it relies on the assumptions that the query words are concrete enough to be visualized, a good search engine can find the images representing the meaning of query words, and we have a pre-trained image recognizer for those images. 

Comparing DIVE with semi-supervised approaches is not the focus of our experiments. Reviewing the hypernym detection methods (including supervised or semi-supervised ones) is not the intention of our experiments. Thanks for pointing out the presentation is potentially confusing. We have moved the comparison to supplementary materials and make our meaning clearer when describing the results. In old Table 1 (now moved to Table 8), the main purpose of showing semi-supervised performances, which are copied from other papers, is to verify the practicality of applying unsupervised methods such as DIVE on the low resource setting. 


Comment 2: It's unclear why only one baseline is included in each case in Table 1.

Response 2: Thanks for the suggestion. We have added the performance of Gaussian embedding on all datasets using the same training and testing setup in new Table 1.


Comment 3: Why use WaCkypedia? It would be interesting to try all scoring functions and types of model (PPMI, PPMI with shift, PPMI with inclusion shift) trained on the exact same corpus and same negatives.

Response 3: WaCkypedia is one of the standard datasets researchers use to train the models when performing hypernym detection (e.g. Vilnis & McCallum, 2015; Athiwaratkun & Wilson, 2017; Baroni et al., 2012; Santus et al., 2014; Santus et al., 2017). 

We did try SBOW PPMI with shift, max(PMI-log(k),0), but we found that larger k usually implies the worse performance. Thanks for reminding us. We have added this explanation to Section 6.2.1. We have applied all scoring functions we mentioned in the second experiment to DIVE, SBOW Freq, SBOW PPMI, SBOW PPMI with inclusion shift. We found that the best scoring functions for SBOW Freq and PPMI are also the best scoring functions for DIVE, so we choose to show those representative scoring functions in Table 4 where all methods are trained on the exact same corpus. They are all unsupervised methods, so we do not train on any negative samples in the testing data.


Comment 4: General question: Is Vendrov's test set only yes/no, e.g. if I set the threshold really low, I get 100% accuracy, or does it contain negatives?

Response 4: All datasets except HyperLex have negative samples (i.e. two words which do not have hypernym relation). For these datasets, we use AP@all (average precision) to evaluate DIVE and baselines, which is the same as AUC (area under precision and recall curve) if constant interpolation is used. AP is computed by averaging the precision of multiple thresholds, and there is no place to set the threshold manually.


Comment 5: What are the novelty and general impact on the field?

Response 5: 
Like many other important and widely used methods, DIVE might look simple and obvious after being proposed and well explained. Nevertheless, we have introduced these skip-gram modifications to several researchers who have done hypernym detection before, and no one understands why the method works (let alone coming up with the same method at the first place) before we introduce the theory that justifies the motivation. Thus, we believe it is safe to say the novelty is high enough.

In this work, we not only propose and theoretically justify a novel unsupervised embedding, which effectively compresses SBOW and significantly outperform previous unsupervised embeddings, but also propose several scoring functions which demonstrate that previous literature usually underestimates the performance of unsupervised methods. DIVE could become one of the important baselines of semi-supervised approaches, especially when the training data are limited, and potentially become one of the components of new semi-supervised approaches.

replying_to: Replying to Distributional Inclusion Vector Embedding for Unsupervised Hypernymy Detection

content.title: Clever model, problematic experiments
content.review:
This paper presents a new method for detecting hypernymy by extending the distributional inclusion hypothesis to low-rank embeddings.

The first half of the paper is written superbly, providing a sober account of the state-of-the-art in hypernymy detection via distributional semantics, and a clear, well-motivated explanation of the main algorithm (DIVE). The reformulation of PMI is interesting; the authors essentially replace P(w) with the uniform distribution (this should be stated explicitly in the paper, BTW). They then augment SGNS to reflect this change by dynamically selecting the number of negatively-sampled contexts according to the target word (w). This is a clever trick.

I was also very happy to see that the authors evaluated on virtually every lexical inference dataset available. However, the remainder of the paper describing the experiments and their results was extremely difficult to parse. First of all, the line between the authors' contribution and prior art is blurry, because they seem to be introducing new metrics for measuring hypernymy as part of the experiments. There are also too many moving parts: datasets, evaluation metrics, detection metrics, embedding methods, hyperparameters, etc. These need to be organized, controlled for, and clearly explained.

I have two major concerns regarding the experiments, beyond intelligibility. First, the authors used a specific corpus (with specific preprocessing) to train their vectors, but compared their results to those reported in other papers, which are not based on the same data. This invalidates these comparisons. Instead, the other methods should be replicated and rerun on exactly the same corpus. I would also recommend using a much larger corpus, since 50M tokens is considered quite small when training word embeddings.

My second concern is that summation (dS) is doing all the heavy lifting. In Table 2, we can see that the difference is only 0.1 between dS and W * dS (where W is also not trained using DIVE). Since dS is basically a proxy for difference in word frequency, could it be that the proposed method is just computing which word is more general? This looks awfully familiar to Levy et al's prototypical hypernym result.

Miscellaneous Comments:
- There's a very recent paper on using vector norms for detecting hypernymy that might be worth contrasting with: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1710.06371.pdf 
- Micro-averaging these datasets is problematic, because some of the datasets based on WordNet are much larger than the hand-annotated ones, and will likely drown them out. Because these datasets are so different, I think it is critical to look at the details and not only at the averages.
- PMI filtering needs to be controlled/ablated in the experiments.
- While explaining equation 6, the authors say that the gradients for x and y are similar; this is not true, because k is a function of x (or y), and if one appears more often in general (not necessarily with c), then the gradients will be different as well.
content.confidence: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature

display_title: New controlled experiments and analysis of old results verified the effectiveness of DIVE

content.title: New controlled experiments and analysis of old results verified the effectiveness of DIVE
content.comment:
Comment 1: Baselines does not use the same training corpus invalidates the comparison. Recommendation of using larger training corpus. PMI filtering needs to be controlled/ablated in the experiments.

Response 1: Thanks for the suggestions. As far as we know, there are only two unsupervised representations which are used to perform unsupervised hypernym detection: Gaussian embedding (GE) and SBOW. We have added the performance of GE on all datasets using the same training and testing setup to new Table 1, where its hyper-parameters are tuned by following the suggestions from the first author of GE. As for SBOW, we have already compared DIVE with them comprehensively using the same experimental setting in Table 4. Comparing DIVE with semi-supervised approaches is not the focus of our paper, so we move it to the supplementary section (see the response to the reviewer 1 below for more details).

Larger corpus does not necessarily give us the better performance. We have found that training on only 50M tokens performs better than training on the whole WaCkypedia for both DIVE and SBOW in almost all datasets, so we choose to compare the methods on the training corpus which gives us the better performances.

We found that PMI filter usually makes SBOW PPMI worse, especially when using more aggressive filtering (larger k). For SBOW Freq, PMI filter will significantly decrease performances of inclusion scoring functions and only slightly increase W*dS and C*dS. Thus, we just compare SBOW PPMI and SBOW Freq w/o PMI filtering with DIVE plus PMI filtering in Table 4. We have added this explanation in the revised Section 6.2.1.


Comment 2: It is critical to look at the details and not only at the micro-averages.

Response 2: We agree that every dataset is unique and informative, so we choose to show performances of all the datasets in Table 1 and Table 4, and we can see DIVE performs constantly well in most of the datasets.


Comment 3: dS is doing all the heavy lifting

Response 3: As mentioned in your previous comment, we should look at the performances of each dataset instead of only looking at the average. In Table 4, you can see C*dS or W*dS is significantly (~2%-10%) better than dS in many datasets (BLESS, Medical, LEDS, TM14, Kotlerman 2010, WordNet, and HyperLex) and performs similarly or worse on the other datasets (EVALution, Lenci/Benotto, Weeds, and HyperNet). The main reason that C*dS or W*dS does not outperform dS in those datasets is simple: The negative samples in those datasets (EVALution, Lenci/Benotto, Weeds, and HyperNet) come from a pair of similar or related words. That is, the datasets are deliberately created to emphasize the generality measurement and decrease the effectiveness of similarity measurement. In practice, the negative samples usually not only include two similar words but also two random words (e.g. BLESS), so generality and similarity signal should both be preserved. Table 4 shows that DIVE did this pretty well.


Comment 4: Introducing new metrics for measuring hypernymy complicates comparison. There are also too many moving parts: datasets, evaluation metrics, detection metrics, embedding methods, hyperparameters, etc. 

Response 4: We propose several new scoring functions (i.e. detection metrics) for two reasons: 
1) From Table 2 and 3, we know that existing scoring functions on SBOW do not perform constantly well on all datasets. By the way, the performance on Table 2 comes from SBOW Freq instead of DIVE.
2) As mentioned in your previous comment, the naive approach such as counting word frequency can achieve decent (although not the best) performance on dS, W*dS, and even CDE, but it does not actually model the pairwise hypernym relations between words. Thus, we need new scoring mechanisms to actually verify that the inclusion property is actually preserved as we claimed theoretically, so we propose AL_1.

We understand that we can do a better job explaining these complicated moving parts, and we will try to achieve that in the future version.


Comment 5: While explaining equation 6, the authors say that the gradients for x and y are similar; this is not true, because k is a function of x (or y), and if one appears more often in general (not necessarily with c), then the gradients will be different as well.

Response 5: DIVE replaces k' in skip-grams by k*Z/#(w), where k is a constant hyper-parameter, so k in equation 6 (note that k is not k’) does not depend on the #(x) or #(y). We did not say the gradients of x and y are similar. Instead, we said the gradients of y (i.e. hypernym/more general words) tend to be equal or higher than the gradient of x. We are doing gradient ascent here, so the embedding of y tends to be larger at the end.

display_title: Interesting approach, but paper needs to improve in presentation and experiments

content.title: Interesting approach, but paper needs to improve in presentation and experiments
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection
content.review:
This paper presents DIVE, a unsupervised method to learn word embeddings while respecting the distributional inclusion hypothesis (DIH). DIH suggests that the context of a hypernym tends to contain the context of its hyponyms. DIVE may be thought of as a unsupervised and direction-reversed version of previously proposed order embeddings. DIVE captures the DIH  heuristic requirement by posing the embedding learning problem as a NMF problem. Modulo construction of the input matrix, the method is quite similar to other word embedding methods like GloVe.

This is overall an ok paper, but I have a few concerns. Firstly, even though the authors have explained in Sec 2.1 how the inclusion constraints are incorporated in the matrix factorization itself, it is not very clear. The authors need to do a better job in improving clarity in this part.

Secondly, and more importantly, I am not sure why SBOW is used as a baseline, even other unsupervised embeddings such Word2Vec or GloVe are readily available and likely to perform better than SBOW. This is a serious limitation which makes it really hard to evaluate true significance of the results.

Thirdly, the fact that all baselines are not applied on all or most of the datasets is unsatisfactory. I think the paper will improve significantly if an uniform evaluation is presented.
content.confidence: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature

content.title: Table 1 has been updated
content.comment:
Response 1: Thanks for telling us the section 2.1 is not clear enough. We will try our best to make it clearer in the future version.

Response 2: In fact, in the appendix (old Table 11), the original submission has already provided the performance of Word2Vec in every dataset we tested. Thanks for letting us know the importance of the comparison. We have moved the results to Table 1 in the revised version. 
By comparing old Table 11 (now Table 1) and Table 4, we can see SBOW significantly outperforms Word2Vec on at least 9 out of 11 datasets. Indeed, when being used to measure the symmetric similarity between words, Word2Vec are usually better than SBOW. However, in this paper, we focus on the unsupervised hypernym detection task, which is a kind of asymmetric relation between words. Previous studies (Nguyen et al., 2017) and our experiments show that Word2Vec does not model such asymmetric relation well, which is one of the main motivations in our paper.

Response 3: Thanks for the suggestion. As far as we know, there are only two unsupervised representations which are used to perform unsupervised hypernym detection: Gaussian embedding (GE) and SBOW. We have added the performance of GE on all datasets using the same training and testing setup in new Table 1, where its hyper-parameters are tuned by following the suggestions from the author of GE. As for SBOW, we have already compared DIVE with them comprehensively using the same experimental setting in Table 4.
Finally, there is no fair way to compare an unsupervised approach like DIVE with semi-supervised approaches, so it is not the focus of the paper. We have moved this comparison to supplementary materials and make the description clearer. The reason we put semi-supervised results on old Table 1 (now Table 8) is just that we want to show that unsupervised approach can sometimes achieve the similar performance compared with semi-supervised method when the number of annotated samples are small.
